questions.question: How do if, for, and switch work in Go?
questions.title: Control flow with if, for, and switch
questions.direct_answer: Go uses `if` for decisions, `for` for repetition, and `switch` for choosing between several related cases. `for` is Go's only loop keyword, and a `switch` stops after the first matching case unless `fallthrough` is written explicitly. Choose the construct that expresses the rule most clearly.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Go's basic control-flow tools and can choose the clearest one for a condition, loop, or set of cases.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Looking for separate while and do-while keywords, or adding `break` after every switch case as in some other languages.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that `for` covers every loop form in Go and that an expressionless switch can replace a long if-else chain.

sections.title: What the interviewer wants
sections.content: Explain the job of `if`, `for`, and `switch`, then show how you choose between them. Mention one Go-specific rule, such as `for` being the only loop keyword or switch cases not falling through automatically.

sections.title: Remember
items: Go has one loop keyword: for.
A switch stops after the first matching case by default.
Prefer the construct that makes the rule easiest to read.

sections.title: Interview answer

beats.spokenText: `if` runs a block when a Boolean condition is true, `for` repeats a block, and `switch` chooses one matching case from several possibilities. Together, they control which statements run and how often they run.

items.label: Control flow
items.detail: Decides what the program does next.

items.label: if
items.detail: Run code only when a condition is true.

items.label: for
items.detail: Run code while a condition or range continues.

items.label: switch
items.detail: Select a clear path from related cases.

beats.spokenText: an `if` can validate an age, a `for` loop can print three values, and a `switch` can handle states such as ready or waiting. Go does not require parentheses around conditions, but braces are required.

support.title: Three familiar shapes
support.caption: The syntax stays small; the construct communicates the intention.

beats.leadIn: I choose between them by asking
beats.spokenText: Choose from the shape of the requirement: one decision suggests `if`, repeated work suggests `for`, and several related alternatives suggest `switch`. Named switch cases are often easier to scan than a long if-else chain.

Use the simplest construct that makes the path obvious. `for` is Go's only loop keyword and covers both while-style loops and `range`. A switch stops after its first matching case; `fallthrough` should appear only when the next case must deliberately run.
beats.recallRule: one decision → `if`; repeated work → `for`; several related cases → `switch`.

items.label: while-style loop
items.detail: There is no separate `while` keyword.

items.label: multiple conditions
items.detail: An expressionless switch can replace chained conditions.

items.label: case behaviour
items.detail: No automatic fall-through in ordinary cases.

sections.content:
- In Go, `if` makes a decision, `for` repeats work, and `switch` chooses between several related cases. These constructs control which statements run next.

- Use `if` when a block should run only if a Boolean condition is true. Go does not require parentheses around the condition, but braces are required. An optional short statement can appear before the condition, and a value declared there is scoped to the if-else chain.

- `for` is Go's only loop keyword. It supports the usual three-part form, a condition-only form similar to `while`, an endless loop written as `for {}`, and `for range` for strings, arrays, slices, maps, and channels.

- Use `switch` when several related cases are easier to read than a long if-else chain. Go evaluates cases from top to bottom and stops after the first match by default, so ordinary cases do not need `break`.

- My rule is simple: one decision suggests `if`, repetition suggests `for`, and a set of named alternatives suggests `switch`. I choose the version that makes the business rule easiest for the next developer to understand.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
Go uses `if` for decisions, `for` for repetition, and `switch` for choosing between several related cases.

`for` is Go's only loop keyword, and a `switch` stops after the first matching case unless `fallthrough` is written explicitly.

Choose the construct that expresses the rule most clearly.

Common mistakes include writing an endless loop accidentally, expecting switch cases to fall through, hiding errors in deeply nested conditions, and misunderstanding variables created inside `if` or `switch`. Keep branches shallow, make loop exits visible, and test boundary conditions.

sections.title: What the interviewer wants
sections.content: Give a practical selection rule for `if`, `for`, and `switch`. Use a small request-handling example and explain why clarity, not cleverness, should guide the choice.

sections.title: Interview answer

beats.spokenText: to use `if` for a direct condition, `for` for repeated work, and `switch` for several related alternatives. The goal is not to use every construct; it is to make the path through the code obvious.

items.label: Question
items.detail: What kind of control does the code need?

items.label: Condition
items.detail: One decision or an early return.

items.label: Repetition
items.detail: Count, continue, or range over data.

items.label: Alternatives
items.detail: Several related cases.

beats.spokenText: a request handler can use an early `if` to reject an invalid role, `range` to inspect permissions, and a `switch` to choose behaviour for active, pending, or blocked accounts. Each construct communicates a different intention.

support.title: A clear selection
support.caption: The shape of the requirement chooses the construct.

beats.spokenText: Guard-clause `if` statements keep nesting shallow, the condition-only form of `for` provides a while-style loop, and `for range` iterates over collections. An expressionless `switch` is useful when several Boolean conditions form one readable decision.

Choose the version a reader can verify fastest. A simple two-branch decision usually remains an `if`, while a long chain of related cases is often clearer as a switch. Readability matters more than a theoretical syntax preference.
beats.recallRule: condition → `if`; repetition → `for`; related alternatives → `switch`; then choose the clearest readable form.

items.label: Two branches
items.detail: Direct and familiar.

items.label: Many named cases
items.detail: Easier to scan and extend.

items.label: A collection
items.detail: Expresses iteration directly.

sections.content:
- Use `if` for a direct Boolean decision or an early return, `for` when work repeats, and `switch` when several related cases belong to the same decision.

- Prefer guard clauses when they remove unnecessary nesting. Use `for range` for collections and a condition-only `for` for while-style loops. An expressionless `switch` can make several related conditions easier to scan.

- These constructs can sometimes express the same logic, so there is no universal winner. Choose the smallest form that communicates the business rule clearly.

sections.title: Make the choice confidently
sections.content:

`for` is Go's only loop keyword, and a `switch` stops after the first matching case unless `fallthrough` is written explicitly.

Use `if` for a direct true-or-false decision, `for` for repeated work, and `switch` for several related cases. The constructs can sometimes express the same logic, so choose the one that makes the intention easiest to understand.

Common mistakes include writing an endless loop accidentally, expecting switch cases to fall through, hiding errors in deeply nested conditions, and misunderstanding variables created inside `if` or `switch`. Keep branches shallow, make loop exits visible, and test boundary conditions.

sections.title: Small example
Important trade-off
sections.content: Use `if` or `if-else` for a small number of unrelated Boolean decisions. Use `switch` when one value, type, or group of related conditions leads to several named outcomes. They can express the same logic, so readability and maintainability decide the choice.

questions.question: What common mistakes should you avoid with Go control flow?
questions.title: Common control-flow mistakes in Go
questions.direct_answer: Common mistakes include writing an endless loop accidentally, expecting switch cases to fall through, hiding errors in deeply nested conditions, and misunderstanding variables created inside `if` or `switch`. Keep branches shallow, make loop exits visible, and test boundary conditions.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you recognise the control-flow errors that produce wrong paths, endless loops, or confusing scope problems.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Listing syntax rules without showing how one of them changes program behaviour.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Trace one input through the condition and name the test that would catch the mistake.

sections.title: What the interviewer wants
sections.content: Name the mistakes that are specific to Go, show one failing loop or branch, and explain the simple habits that prevent it.

sections.title: Interview answer

beats.spokenText: Control flow decides which statements run and how often they run. In Go, `if` handles conditions, `for` handles repetition, and `switch` handles related alternatives. Bugs appear when the written path does not match the intended path.

items.label: Control flow
items.detail: The written path and intended path must match.

items.label: if
items.detail: Runs a block when its condition is true.

items.label: for
items.detail: Must progress toward an exit unless intentionally endless.

items.label: switch
items.detail: Stops after the matching case by default.

beats.spokenText: A condition-only loop can run forever if the value tested by the condition never changes. In this example, forgetting `retries++` means `retries < 3` always remains true, so the request is sent repeatedly.

support.title: The state must move toward the exit
support.caption: Check which statement makes the loop condition eventually become false.

beats.spokenText: A normal switch stops after the first matching case, and a value declared in an `if` initializer exists only in that if-else chain. `fallthrough` enters the next case without checking its condition, so it should appear only when that behaviour is deliberate.

items.label: Is the variable used within its scope?

beats.cue: Keep control flow easy to verify
beats.spokenText: Keep the happy path shallow, name loop state clearly, and test both sides of every important boundary. Loop tests should cover zero, one, and maximum iterations; switch tests should cover every case and the default path.
beats.recallRule: make loop progress visible, remember switch does not fall through, and test every boundary and default path.

support.title: Test the path, not only the result

items.label: Loop boundary
items.detail: Catches missed and extra iterations.

items.label: Switch
items.detail: Catches missing alternatives.

items.label: Nested branch
items.detail: Keeps the main path visible.

sections.content:
- Make sure a loop changes the state used by its condition; otherwise it may never finish.

- Go switch cases stop automatically. Use `fallthrough` only deliberately because it enters the next case without testing that case's condition.

- Values declared in an `if` or `switch` initializer stay inside that statement. Keep important paths shallow with early returns, and test loop boundaries plus every switch case and default.

questions.question: When should you use switch instead of if-else in Go?
questions.title: Go switch versus if-else
questions.direct_answer: Use `if` or `if-else` for a small number of unrelated Boolean decisions. Use `switch` when one value, type, or group of related conditions leads to several named outcomes. They can express the same logic, so readability and maintainability decide the choice.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can compare if-else and switch using the shape and readability of a real decision.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Claiming that switch is always faster instead of explaining that the compiler and case shape determine implementation details.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention expressionless and type switches as useful Go forms, while keeping a simple two-branch decision as if-else.

sections.title: What the interviewer wants
sections.content: Compare the two forms using the same decision. Explain where each reads better and avoid unsupported performance claims.

sections.title: Interview answer

beats.spokenText: choose which block runs. An `if-else` chain evaluates Boolean conditions in order, while a `switch` groups related cases under one decision. The real difference is usually how clearly the code communicates those alternatives.

items.label: Decision
items.detail: Select one path from the available paths.

items.label: if-else
items.detail: Good for a few unrelated checks.

items.label: switch
items.detail: Good for related alternatives.

items.label: Main trade-off
items.detail: Choose what is easiest to scan.

beats.spokenText: three account states can be written as repeated equality checks, but a switch puts the decision value in one place and makes the valid cases easy to scan. A two-branch check such as valid or invalid is usually simpler as `if-else`.

support.title: Several related values
support.code:
switch status {
case "active":
    allow()
case "pending":
    review()
case "blocked":
    deny()
default:
    reportUnknown()
}
support.caption: The switch keeps the subject and its cases together.

beats.spokenText: an expressionless `switch` for related Boolean conditions and a type switch for behaviour based on an interface value's dynamic type. These forms are useful when they name one coherent decision, not simply to avoid writing `if`.

Keep `if-else` for one or two direct conditions and choose `switch` when multiple cases belong to the same question. Do not promise a speed difference without measurement because the compiler and the case values determine the generated code.
beats.recallRule: few direct conditions → `if-else`; several related values, conditions, or types → `switch`.

items.label: One or two checks
items.detail: Short and direct.

items.label: Many related cases
items.detail: Keeps alternatives together.

items.label: Performance claim
items.detail: Do not guess from syntax alone.

sections.content:
- Both `if-else` and `switch` choose which code runs. Use `if-else` for a few direct or unrelated conditions and `switch` when several cases answer the same question.

- Go supports value switches, expressionless switches for Boolean conditions, and type switches for interface values. Normal switch cases stop automatically.

- The choice is mainly about readability. Do not claim one form is always faster without measuring the actual code.

sections.title: Understand the decision
sections.content:
Go uses `if` for decisions, `for` for repetition, and `switch` for choosing between several related cases.

`for` is Go's only loop keyword, and a `switch` stops after the first matching case unless `fallthrough` is written explicitly.

Use `if` or `if-else` for a small number of unrelated Boolean decisions. Use `switch` when one value, type, or group of related conditions leads to several named outcomes. They can express the same logic, so readability and maintainability decide the choice.

Common mistakes include writing an endless loop accidentally, expecting switch cases to fall through, hiding errors in deeply nested conditions, and misunderstanding variables created inside `if` or `switch`. Keep branches shallow, make loop exits visible, and test boundary conditions.

sections.title: Small example
sections.content:
```go
switch status {
case Active:
    allow()
case Pending:
    review()
default:
    deny()
}
```

questions.question: How would you debug incorrect control flow in Go?
questions.title: Debugging incorrect control flow in Go
questions.direct_answer: Reproduce the smallest failing input, write down the expected path, and trace each condition and loop-state change. Check boundaries, early returns, switch defaults, and whether a loop can reach its exit. Fix the rule rather than the symptom, then add a focused regression test.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can turn a wrong branch or loop result into a small, testable execution trace.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding more conditions before identifying which existing condition selected the wrong path.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: State the expected path first, then show the exact value that makes actual execution diverge.

sections.title: What the interviewer wants
sections.content: Describe a repeatable debugging flow: reproduce, trace, locate the first wrong decision, fix the rule, and protect it with a boundary test.

sections.title: Interview answer

beats.cue: Reduce the failure to one path
beats.spokenText: Find the smallest input that produces the wrong result and write down the expected path. Then trace the actual condition values, selected switch case, early return, and loop state until the two paths first differ.

items.label: Expected path
items.detail: Write the intended branches before changing code.

items.label: Input
items.detail: Use the smallest failing value.

items.label: Actual path
items.detail: Record every decision result.

items.label: First difference
items.detail: Later symptoms are consequences.

beats.spokenText: if a score of 80 should be classified as high but the code checks `score > 80`, the boundary follows the default path. A table test containing 79, 80, and 81 makes the incorrect operator immediately visible.

support.title: Test around the boundary
support.code:
switch {
case score >= 80:
    return "high"
case score >= 50:
    return "medium"
default:
    return "low"
}
support.caption: The corrected comparison includes the exact boundary value.

beats.spokenText: whether conditions cover equality boundaries, whether an early return skips required work, whether a switch needs a default case, and whether every loop either changes its controlling state or deliberately waits for an event.

beats.cue: Fix the rule and prove it
beats.spokenText: Make the smallest change that corrects the decision and add a regression test for the failing value. Run the neighbouring boundary values and the normal path as well, so the fix does not simply move the bug to another branch.
beats.recallRule: expected path → actual trace → first divergence → smallest fix → boundary regression test.

items.label: Before the fix
items.detail: Prove which decision is wrong.

items.label: The fix
items.detail: Correct the rule, not a later symptom.

items.label: After the fix
items.detail: Cover below, at, and above the boundary.

sections.content:
- Start with the smallest failing input and write down the expected sequence of branches. Trace actual condition values until execution first takes a different path.

- Check equality boundaries, early returns, switch defaults, loop progress, and loop exits. These are common places where the written rule differs from the intended rule.

- Make the smallest correction and add a table-driven regression test containing the failing value plus its neighbouring boundary values.

sections.title: Why the mistake happens
sections.content:

`for` is Go's only loop keyword, and a `switch` stops after the first matching case unless `fallthrough` is written explicitly.

Use `if` for a direct true-or-false decision, `for` for repeated work, and `switch` for several related cases. The constructs can sometimes express the same logic, so choose the one that makes the intention easiest to understand.

Reproduce the smallest failing input, write down the expected path, and trace each condition and loop-state change. Check boundaries, early returns, switch defaults, and whether a loop can reach its exit. Fix the rule rather than the symptom, then add a focused regression test.

sections.content:
```go
tests := []struct { score int; want string }{
    {79, "medium"},
    {80, "high"},
    {81, "high"},

```
